Q: How to get remote json metadata by javascript avoiding Cross-Origin Request Blocked A:

The key issue here is "Cross-Origin". It's a security mechanism that doesn't allow one webpage to read the contents of another webpage (on a different domain) without its explicit consent. So when you open the link in your browser directly, it's not "cross resource" and everything works fine.

CORS can cause many problems when first learning about it, you can read a good description of it ad mdn:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

Reading a static file (as far as I know) does not add the required headers by default. If you don't own the server you're trying to read from and they don't offer another endpoint that allows CORS, then it won't be possible. If you do control the server you're requesting, have a look atthe examples how to enable cors https://enable-cors.org/index.html

Q: Create a list of console_scripts defined in a Python package A:

pkg_resources was deprecated several years ago and was removed as of setuptools 82.0.0.

The replacements is using importlib.resources.entry_points :

from importlib.resources import entry_points

def find_console_scripts(package_name):
    entrypoints = [
        ep for ep in entry_points(group="console_scripts")
        if ep.value.partition(".")[0] == package_name
    ]
    return entrypoints

Q: How do I serialize a floating point number? A:

I'm sure there are duplicates of this question, but just as a quick answer: Yes, IEEE-754 is standardized enough that a simple memcpy works fine and you only need to worry about endianness. They are called IEEE-754 interchange formats. See e.g. What does The IEEE-754 mean by "interchange formats"?

To be specific, the 32 and 64 bit formats (plus some others, less often used ones) have a defined bit pattern from most to least significant bit. Therefore endianness is relevant. See e.g. Converting float values from big endian to little endian

For C++ specifically, you can also check whether your environment uses IEEE-754, though this is mostly a given these days. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/numeric_limits/is_iec559.html. For C99, the check is covered here: Ensuring C++ doubles are 64 bits

In practical terms I suggest:

  1. You memcpy
  2. Adjust or specify endianness
  3. Build a static_assert or similar compilation error if the hardware does not use IEEE-754. This will probably never trigger on real hardware. One may hope that any diverging platform supports converting to the IEEE formats.

The reason I advocate for this is that it optimizes for the common case rather than wasting cycles (and heat and energy) on a more complex conversion that is only really relevant for niche platforms. The IEEE-754 bit pattern is well documented. If your code is ever ported to one of those platforms, you can invest the time and CPU cycles converting to their native formats at that point.

Additional gotchas

While irrelevant in most use cases, I have to point out three more issues:

  1. NaN payloads are not standardized but for the most part can simply be ignored

  2. The bit pattern for signalling vs. quiet NaNs is not standardized and in fact flipped on some platforms. You cannot solve this in the serializing step. You have to solve it in the deserializing step.

    A simple if(isnan(x)) x = NAN; solves the problem by turning all NaNs into a canonical quiet NaN, also dropping any payload in the process.

  3. Some platforms, most notably the smallest Arduino UNO don't support double and treat double as an alias to float.

    Again, this is something that should be caught by the static_assert or similar and then require software conversion from double to float; or simply remain a compile error if you deem that the loss of range and precision cannot be quietly tolerated

Q: What is recommended for merge the working tree file with the stash file? A:

Stage your file, then apply the stash. Be aware that if you run into any conflicts, your local (uncommitted) changes might be lost.

Or just commit your changes, then apply the stash. You can always undo (git reset HEAD^) the commit later.

Q: Architecture for handling OAuth token refresh across multiple services in agent-based systems A:

A few behaviors to consider.

TOKEN REFRESH

Only user-facing clients (e.g. a browser app or mobile app) should initiate token refresh requests. Multiple views or frontend workers must synchronise token refresh, e.g.:

  • Queue up a collection of promises.
  • Only the first promise runs a refresh.
  • All promises return the same refresh result.

The result should be short-lived tokens (or cookies that represent tokens), e.g. with a 15 minute lifetime. The short lifetime helps to mitigate token (or cookie) interception threats.

BACKEND WORKLOADS

These should not need to synchronise and each replica should receive user-level access tokens when a user is present. That keeps user attributes cryptographically verifiable and auditable.

When no user is present, e.g. for a nightly job, backend replicas can each get their own access token with the same client credential, without conflicts.

TOKEN EXCHANGE

A common option is to receive an access token from an internet client. For example, a web portal could use the A2A protocol to send a natural language command to a backend agent.

However, the web portal may have more scopes than you want the agent to receive. Therefore, an API gateway can use OAuth Token Exchange to downscope the access token before routing to the agent. Doing so maintains user identity attributes within the exchanged token.

Token exchange is often accompanied by in-memory caching. For example, with the hash of the original user-level access token as the cache key and the exchanged token as the cache value.

FEDERATION

Ideally. token exchange should span organizations, each of which could implement the Identity Assertion Grant, a federated form of token exchange.

When that is not possible, you may need to get a third-party token in other ways, e.g with the client credentials grant. You may be able to continue to use an incoming access token as a cache key, so that you keep third-party tokens in the backend.

SUMMARY

In OAuth, an up to date authorization server should issue tokens that enable the following behaviours, none of which should require complex code:

  • Frontend components use token refresh to balance good usability with short-lived HTTP credentials.

  • Resource servers use access tokens from their trusted issuer, and you can dictate scopes and claims that each client and resource server receives in access tokens.

  • Token exchange enables you to control tokens, to change their scopes and claims, as tokens flow between backend components.

If agents ever behave unpredictably, and try to perform operations outside of their remit, token attributes should enable resource servers to deny access.
